title: The Criminologist's Son: Cocaine, the Analysis of Jung, and the War Against the Father
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Gniebing-Weissenbach, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; the village coordinates are approximate, the Feldbach district of eastern Styria
stops.campa: In a Styrian village east of Graz a son is born to Hans Gross, the examining magistrate who is building the science of criminal investigation out of fingerprints, fibres and the habits of thieves. The father spends his working life proving that a disordered man leaves marks on the world around him. The son will spend his own arguing the reverse: that the world, and above all the family, leaves the marks, and that what psychiatry calls disorder is the print of the father's thumb. The date on the register is the seventeenth of March, 1877.
suggested_refs: Parish and civil birth registers of Gniebing-Weissenbach, Styria, 17 March 1877

stops.name: Graz, the household of Hans Gross
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1881; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: From his fourth year the household stands in Graz, a provincial capital of gymnasiums and garrisons, where his father's reputation grows into a European one. Criminalistics is invented at this address: the method by which a state learns to read guilt from the objects a suspect touched. The boy is raised inside that method, taught which categories exist and how they are applied. Every school he attends and every examination he sits will be in his father's town. He learns them thoroughly.
suggested_refs: The Graz residence of Hans Gross, professor of criminal law and founder of criminalistics

stops.name: Graz, the Matura and the change of faculty
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1894; month and day defaulted to the summer examination season
stops.campa: He passes the Matura at the second imperial and royal state gymnasium and enrolls, to nobody's satisfaction, in zoology and botany. Within the year he has changed to medicine, and will take the degree at Graz five years later. Later tellers of the story supply a father insisting on it, and the insistence fits the shape of everything that follows, but no reachable document gives a reason. What the record holds is a seventeen year old moving from beetles and plants to anatomy. Nobody wrote down why.
suggested_refs: The 2. k.u.k. Staatsgymnasium, Graz, matriculation records for 1894

stops.name: Munich, the summer semester of 1897
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summer semester of 1897; the day is defaulted
stops.campa: In the summer semester of 1897 he transfers to Munich, and from there to Strasbourg, and back to Graz, stitching a medical training across three faculties rather than completing it in one. Munich will matter to him enormously later, as Schwabing and as Kraepelin's clinic; now it is a lecture hall he passes through at twenty. He sits the examinations wherever he happens to be that term, and leaves the registrars to work out afterwards which faculty is holding his file.
suggested_refs: Matriculation rolls of the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitaet and the University of Strasbourg, 1897-1899

stops.name: Graz, the doctorate in medicine
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1899; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He takes the Dr. med. at Graz in 1899, twenty-two years old, trained across three cities and returned to the one his father owns. The degree entitles him to practise, to lecture in time, to hold a post in any asylum in the monarchy. He is quick, and already impatient with the classificatory psychiatry he has been handed, which sorts human beings into diagnostic bins the way his father sorts evidence into envelopes. The next year he goes to sea as a ship's physician.
suggested_refs: Promotion records of the medical faculty, Karl-Franzens-Universitaet Graz, 1899

stops.name: Valparaiso, the ship's medicine chest
stops.date_confidence: the 1900 voyage and the onset of cocaine use are attested; the specific port is reconstruction, since the Kosmos line called at several Chilean and Peruvian harbours
stops.campa: He signs on as ship's physician with the Kosmos line of Hamburg, bound for the Pacific coast of South America, and comes home with the thing that will govern the rest of his life. Long crossings, a locked chest he holds the key to, and a young doctor with no supervisor within four thousand miles. Cocaine enters here. He is twenty-three. Which harbour he was standing in when it did, no paper says; the line called at Chilean and Peruvian ports all down the coast, and no landing of his is recorded.
suggested_refs: Passenger and crew manifests of the Deutsche Dampfschiffahrtsgesellschaft Kosmos, South America service, 1900

stops.name: Burghoelzli, Zurich: the first cure
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1902; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: After a year as a psychiatric assistant in Munich and in Graz he admits himself to the Burghoelzli, the cantonal asylum above Zurich, for the first of the withdrawal cures. Eugen Bleuler runs the house and is in these years assembling the word schizophrenia. On the staff, unremarked, is an assistant named Carl Jung, two years older than the patient and a long way from anything. He is twenty-five, three years out of his doctorate and two years into the drug. The cure does not take.
suggested_refs: Admission registers of the Burghoelzli cantonal asylum under Eugen Bleuler, 1902

stops.name: Leipzig, Die cerebrale Sekundaerfunction
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1902; month unknown, defaulted. The intake record misplaced this book to Graz and misspelled its title
stops.campa: Vogel of Leipzig prints a short book by the twenty-five year old that divides human minds by the behaviour of consciousness itself: one type shallow and outward and quick to spend itself, the other narrow, deep and turned inward. He builds it out of the clinic, from manic patients set beside paranoid ones. Nineteen years later Jung will name those two types for the century and will print, in plain type, who had them first. Whether he read the book in 1902, in the same building, nothing says.
stops.quote: Gross deserves full credit for being the first to set up a simple and consistent hypothesis to account for this [the extraverted] type.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung, Psychological Types (1921), Collected Works vol. 6, par. 466
suggested_refs: Otto Gross, Die cerebrale Sekundaerfunction (Leipzig: Vogel, 1902)
sources: C. G. Jung, Psychological Types, CW 6, par. 466

stops.name: Graz, the marriage to Frieda Schloffer
stops.date_confidence: attested; the wedding's location in Graz is inferred from both families
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of February he marries Frieda Schloffer, born in Graz in 1876, sister of the surgeon Hermann Schloffer and niece by marriage to the philosopher Alois Riehl. One widely copied account makes her the surgeon's daughter instead, which would have required him to father her at eight. It is, on its face, two respectable Graz families joining. She will follow him to Ascona, bear his legitimate son, and defend him in court against his own father. She outlives him by thirty years and dies at Bosco-Gurin, a mountain village in the Ticino, in December 1950.
suggested_refs: Marriage register, Graz, 23 February 1903; the Schloffer family papers

stops.name: Graz, the Habilitationsschrift submitted
stops.date_confidence: attested that he submitted the Habilitationsschrift in 1905; month and day unknown. The venia is exercised from the winter semester of 1906/07
stops.campa: He submits his habilitation thesis to the faculty at Graz and is on his way to the title of Privatdozent for psychopathology, which is to say a place inside academic medicine at the age of twenty-eight. His father's university, his father's town, his father's method turned to a different use. Four years later he will publish a full monograph on psychopathic inferiorities, the last work he writes from anything resembling a chair. The venia is exercised from the winter semester of 1906/07, by which time he is working in Munich.
suggested_refs: Habilitation file, medical faculty, Karl-Franzens-Universitaet Graz, 1905; Otto Gross, Ueber psychopathische Minderwertigkeiten (Vienna: Braumueller, 1909)

stops.name: Monte Verita, Ascona: the cure by sun
stops.date_confidence: the 1906 Ascona stay is attested; the date given is Lotte Hattemer's death, 19 April 1906. Whether Gross had any part in it is contested
stops.campa: He climbs to the hill above Ascona where Ida Hofmann and Henri Oedenkoven have run a colony of vegetarians and sun-bathers since 1900, and tries to break the drug on light, raw food and air instead of a locked ward. Here he meets Erich Muehsam and Johannes Nohl and finds the anarchism his psychiatry has been missing. That April a settler on the hill, Lotte Hattemer, dies at twenty-nine. One German account says flatly that Gross supplied the poison; the police file of 1909 closes on suicide and carries his part only as rumour.
suggested_refs: The Monte Verita colony above Ascona; the 1906-1909 police file on the death of Lotte Hattemer

stops.name: Munich, assistant to Emil Kraepelin
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the first of September he takes a post under Emil Kraepelin at the Munich psychiatric clinic, the most orthodox appointment of his life. Kraepelin sorts madness by symptom and by course, and his tables are the ones psychiatry still teaches. His new assistant is meanwhile reading Freud against the grain and arriving somewhere neither Freud nor Kraepelin will follow: that neurosis is not a defect in the patient but the stamp the patriarchal family presses into every child it raises. The post does not last long.
suggested_refs: Staff records of the Royal Psychiatric Clinic, Munich, under Emil Kraepelin, 1906

stops.name: Graz, the lecture on Freud's doctrine of ideogenesis
stops.date_confidence: attested for the winter semester of 1906/07; the day is defaulted
stops.campa: In the winter semester he stands up in Graz as Privatdozent and lectures on Freud's doctrine of ideogenesis, that an idea can make a body sick. In 1906 this is not a career move. Vienna's new psychology is a scandal in the German faculties, and the young man announcing it from a lectern in a provincial university is announcing which side he is on. Freud in Vienna hears that he has an advocate inside the Austrian academy. The catalogue prints the course under the title Ueber die Freud'sche Ideogenitaetslehre.
suggested_refs: Lecture catalogue of the University of Graz, winter semester 1906/07: 'Ueber die Freud'sche Ideogenitaetslehre'

segments.name: The Sisters, the Congress, the Wall

stops.name: Schwabing, Munich: the two sisters
stops.date_confidence: 1907 is the year that fits the birth of Else Jaffe's son at the end of that year; one strand of the record dates the affairs to 1906. Month and day unknown
stops.campa: In the cafes and studios of Schwabing he takes up with Else von Richthofen, married to the economist Edgar Jaffe, and with her sister Frieda, married to the philologist Ernest Weekley. Both affairs run at once and neither is hidden, because concealment is the very thing his theory condemns. Frieda will leave Weekley for D. H. Lawrence, and Gross's ideas travel with her into the novels. His own wife bears him a legitimate son this year, and the boy is called Wolfgang Peter.
stops.quote: talked all the time — even, if his portrait in D.H. Lawrence's novel Mr Noon is accurate, during sexual intercourse.
stops.quote_source: Brenda Maddox, Freud's Wizard: The Enigma of Ernest Jones (London: John Murray, 2006), p. 55, on Otto Gross
suggested_refs: D. H. Lawrence, Mr Noon; Martin Green, The von Richthofen Sisters

stops.name: Heidelberg, the son who is given another father
stops.date_confidence: attested for the end of 1907; the day is defaulted and the Heidelberg setting follows the Jaffe household rather than a recorded birth place
stops.campa: Else Jaffe bears a son at the end of the year and the child is entered into the world as Edgar Jaffe's. He is called Peter. The arrangement is the ordinary bourgeois solution to an extraordinary situation, and it holds: the boy grows up inside a marriage, with a name, an address and a father, none of which are his. His actual father is by now advocating in print the abolition of exactly this machinery, and accepts its protection for the boy. Whether Peter was ever told, no reachable document says.
suggested_refs: The Jaffe household at Heidelberg; Martin Green, Else und Frieda (German edition 1976)

stops.name: Salzburg, Hotel Bristol: the congress
stops.date_confidence: attested for 26 and 27 April 1908 in the German record; the English record gives 27 April alone. The meeting was convened as the First Congress for Freudian Psychology, not as an international congress: the association is founded at Nuremberg in 1910
stops.campa: Forty-odd men gather at the Hotel Bristol for the first congress the new psychology has ever held, and Gross stands up to push it where Freud will not go. If repression makes neurosis, he argues, and if the family manufactures repression, then the cure is not an hour on a couch but the end of the patriarchal family itself. Freud has argued the opposite case in print that same year. The room hears a young man turn a therapy into a politics. Freud will see to it that he is pushed out of psychoanalysis and struck from its annals.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the First Congress for Freudian Psychology, Hotel Bristol, Salzburg, 26-27 April 1908

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19: the analysis nobody can prove
stops.date_confidence: the year is a convention. That Freud personally analysed Gross at Berggasse 19 is asserted in parts of the secondary literature and is absent from the German record, which says instead that Freud saw to his expulsion. Reconstruction, flagged
stops.campa: The story runs that Freud takes him into personal analysis at Berggasse 19, an intimacy extended to almost nobody in the movement, and that within a single year both founders of the new psychology try and fail to cure the same man. The story is told and retold and cannot be produced. What the record does hold is colder: that Freud, having taken the opposite position on sexual morality in print, saw to it that Gross was pushed out of psychoanalysis and struck from its annals. Whether he first offered him a couch, the archive does not say.
suggested_refs: Sigmund Freud, Die kulturelle Sexualmoral und die moderne Nervositaet (1908); The Otto Gross - Carl Jung Correspondence
sources: gap noted: no primary text reachable for a Freud analysis of Gross

stops.name: Burghoelzli, Zurich: Jung's patient analyses Jung
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the sixth of May he is admitted to the Burghoelzli again, this time handed to Carl Jung with Freud's blessing and the expectation that Zurich discipline will finish what Vienna could not. The frame gives way almost at once. The two of them sit for days at a stretch and the direction reverses: the patient reads the doctor's repressions back to him with the same fluency the doctor is being paid to use. Freud is told about it by letter, from Zurich, as the sessions run. Jung is thirty-three and has never met anything like it.
stops.quote: Jung claimed his entire worldview changed when he attempted to analyse Gross
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'Otto Gross', summarizing Jung's own account of the 1908 treatment
suggested_refs: The Otto Gross - Carl Jung Correspondence (Princeton); the Freud-Jung letters of May and June 1908

stops.name: Burghoelzli, Zurich: over the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested for the flight on 17 June 1908; the much repeated detail that he went over the garden wall is not in the reachable sources
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of June, six weeks in, he leaves the Burghoelzli without waiting for anyone's permission and does not come back. The much repeated detail that he went over the garden wall is not in the reachable sources; they say only that he fled. Jung, his authority restored by the distance, writes the verdict into the file: dementia praecox. It is the diagnosis that will follow Gross into every asylum he is put in for the next twelve years.
suggested_refs: Jung's case notes and letters on the Gross treatment, May-June 1908

stops.name: Munich, a daughter to Regina Ullmann
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1908; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The poet Regina Ullmann, his patient, bears him a daughter, Camilla. It is 1908, the year of the Burghoelzli and of the flight from it. It is also the third child in two years by three women, one of them his wife and two of them under his care. The theory says the line between physician and lover is one more bourgeois fence around a healthy instinct. The clinic says otherwise, and the clinic writes the references. Of the daughter Camilla the record holds a birth and nothing after it.
suggested_refs: The papers of Regina Ullmann, poet, Munich

stops.name: Ascona, Sophie Benz with child
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1909; the day is defaulted
stops.campa: In October Sophie Benz, his lover and his patient, is carrying his child. She is loved also by the writer Leonhard Frank, and the three of them are living out at Ascona the doctrine of unforced love that Gross has spent five years arguing is the cure for the sickness of Europe. In Vienna this same year Braumueller prints his monograph on psychopathic inferiorities, the last work he writes with a university title still attached to his name. He is still, on paper, Privatdozent for psychopathology at Graz.
suggested_refs: Otto Gross, Ueber psychopathische Minderwertigkeiten (Vienna and Leipzig: Braumueller, 1909)

stops.name: Rab, the island in the Adriatic
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1910; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He takes Sophie Benz to the island of Rab off the Croatian coast, stone and pine and salt water, as far from a clinic as the monarchy allows. On the island her mind gives way. What the witnesses describe is psychosis; what the physician with her does about it, the record does not preserve. She has been carrying his child since the October before. They come back to Ascona in the autumn of 1910. The colony takes them in without asking questions, which is what it was founded to do.
suggested_refs: The island of Rab, Kvarner, in the Gross circle's 1909-1910 travels

stops.name: Ascona, the death of Sophie Benz
stops.date_confidence: attested. The claim that Gross supplied the poison is not in the source that carries the date; in the German record that sentence attaches to Lotte Hattemer
stops.campa: On the third of March Sophie Benz kills herself at Ascona. She had been pregnant by him since the autumn before last and out of her mind since the summer. Whether he supplied the means is not attested: the German record attaches that sentence to Lotte Hattemer, not to her. The colony that had promised a life without coercion has produced, in five years, two dead young women and one physician standing near both of them. Leonhard Frank, who loved her too, will put the three of them in a novel and call Gross Dr. Kreuz.
suggested_refs: Leonhard Frank, Links, wo das Herz ist (1952), in which Gross appears as 'Dr. Kreuz'

stops.name: Mendrisio, the Casvegno house
stops.date_confidence: attested. The German record describes a voluntary admission for treatment, not a committal; the popular literature describes a committal
stops.campa: Three days after the suicide he presents himself at the Casvegno institution at Mendrisio, an hour down the valley from Ascona, and asks for treatment. The German record calls it a voluntary admission; the popular literature calls it a committal. He is still, at this point, a doctor choosing a hospital, giving his own name and his own history at the desk. It is the last time in his life that the door is one he opens himself. Three weeks later he is transferred to Vienna.
suggested_refs: The Casvegno psychiatric institution, Mendrisio, Canton Ticino, admission records for March 1911

stops.name: Am Steinhof, Vienna: the domed city on the hill
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of March he is transferred to Am Steinhof on the western hills of Vienna, sixty pavilions under Otto Wagner's gold dome, opened four years earlier as the most modern asylum in Europe. He arrives as an inmate in the city where the new psychology was made, three years after its founders decided he had no place in it. He is thirty-four, three weeks into institutional care and nine years from the end of it. Eight kilometres of Vienna separate Berggasse 19 from the pavilion he is put in.
suggested_refs: The Otto Wagner hospital complex Am Steinhof, Vienna, patient registers for 1911

stops.name: Berlin, the warrant for poison
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1912; month and day unknown, defaulted. The Berlin location within the city is not recorded
stops.campa: A Berlin court issues a warrant against him for murder and for abetting suicide: he is said to have supplied poison to two women of the city who then tried to kill themselves. Both women survive. It is the third time the same accusation has formed around him, and the first time a court acts on it. His own writing names the family as the murderer and society as the accessory. What address in the city the warrant named, the record does not give. He is not in Berlin to answer either charge.
suggested_refs: Prussian court records, Berlin, 1912, on the charge of murder and abetting suicide

stops.name: Wilmersdorf, Berlin: the Aktion circle
stops.date_confidence: attested for February 1913; the day and the exact Wilmersdorf address are not recorded
stops.campa: In February, warrant and all, he moves to Berlin and takes a room with the writer Franz Jung, who is no relation to the other one, and joins Franz Pfemfert's circle around the journal Die Aktion. Expressionist Berlin gives him what the consulting rooms of Vienna and Zurich have withdrawn: readers who want the politics and not just the diagnosis. For one season the city takes him seriously. What he writes for Pfemfert is that no revolution can succeed which leaves the father at the head of the household.
suggested_refs: Die Aktion, ed. Franz Pfemfert, Berlin, 1913, Gross's contributions

stops.name: Berlin, arrested as a dangerous anarchist
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrest and the expulsion order; the site within Berlin is not recorded
stops.campa: On the ninth of November the Prussian police take him as a dangerous anarchist and order him out of Prussia. His father has been waiting for precisely this. Hans Gross has spent his working life writing the handbooks by which examining magistrates learn to read a suspect's mind. Rather than let the state simply put his son over a border, he uses the arrest to reach for psychiatry, which can finish what a deportation order cannot. The son is thirty-six.
suggested_refs: Prussian police files, Berlin, 9 November 1913, expulsion of Otto Gross

stops.name: Tulln, the private asylum on the Danube
stops.date_confidence: attested for late 1913; the month and day are approximate and the asylum's exact address is not identified
stops.campa: He is shut into a private asylum at Tulln on the Danube at his father's instigation; which house, the record does not name. The press does not let it pass. Erich Muehsam and Franz Pfemfert put the case into every paper that will print it, and the campaign runs into the international press: a son locked up by the man who wrote the rulebook the state uses to lock people up. Austrian psychiatry in 1913 has no test that separates the mad from the merely intolerable. What the campaign argues about, month after month, is which of the two Otto Gross is.
suggested_refs: The 1913-1914 international press campaign for Gross's release, in Die Aktion and elsewhere

stops.name: Troppau, the guardianship
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1914; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The district court at Graz declares him entmuendigt, stripped of legal capacity, on the grounds of profligacy and habitual use of nerve poisons, and appoints his father as his guardian. The wording does not say insane. It says incapable, which for a man of thirty-seven amounts to being made a child again by the one person who wanted it. From Tulln he is moved on to the Landesirrenanstalt at Troppau, in Austrian Silesia, four hundred kilometres from Graz.
suggested_refs: Graz district court, Kuratel proceedings against Otto Gross, 1914; Landesirrenanstalt Troppau admission records

stops.name: Troppau, released as recovered
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eighth of July the asylum discharges him as recovered. The word is a formality and everybody signing it knows so; Muehsam and Pfemfert have run the case in every paper that would take it for the better part of a year, and it has made him too expensive to hold. Twenty days later the empire is at war, and no editor in Vienna has a column to spare for a psychiatrist's guardianship. The guardianship itself is not lifted. He leaves Troppau a discharged patient and a legally incapable man, still under his father's guardianship.
suggested_refs: Discharge record, Landesirrenanstalt Troppau, 8 July 1914

stops.name: Bad Ischl, Stekel and the Kuh sisters
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The day after his discharge his aftercare passes to Wilhelm Stekel, one of Freud's oldest Viennese followers, at a sanatorium in Bad Ischl among the lakes. Two nurses there are sisters of the Viennese writer Anton Kuh: Marianne, born 1893, and Nina, born 1897. Both enter his life. Anton Kuh he will meet later, in Prague, at Max Brod's table. How long the Bad Ischl aftercare lasts, no record reached says. Marianne bears him a daughter, Sophie, in 1916.
suggested_refs: Wilhelm Stekel's sanatorium practice at Bad Ischl, 1914

stops.name: Graz, the death of Hans Gross
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1915; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: His father dies, and the guardianship does not die with him. The court hands it to Anton Rintelen, a Styrian jurist and politician with no personal interest in the case at all, and Gross goes on contesting it in front of judges who have never met him. He has spent seven years arguing that paternal authority survives the individual father and works through institutions instead. The court proves the thesis in a single administrative act. The month of the death is not recorded in anything reachable; the year is 1915. He contests the transfer. He loses.
suggested_refs: Styrian court records on the transfer of the Gross Kuratel to Anton Rintelen, 1915

stops.name: Ungvar, the epidemic barracks
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1915; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The war finds a use for him. At Ungvar in the Carpathian foothills he works the barrack hospitals where typhus and dysentery come down off the front by the trainload. He is thirty-eight and has been legally incapable for a year. The army needs physicians badly enough to overlook a court file, and nobody at Ungvar asks what he was famous for. No theory of matriarchy is called for here. The work is fluids, quarantine, disinfectant, and the counting of the dead.
suggested_refs: Austro-Hungarian military epidemic hospital records, Ungvar (Uzhhorod), 1915

stops.name: Vinkovci, the typhus wards of Slavonia
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1915; the month is approximate and the order of the two postings is not fixed by the record
stops.campa: From the Carpathians the postings take him south to Vinkovci in Slavonia, where he serves as assistant physician, civil and then military, in another epidemic hospital. The file from these years contains a rank, a station and a service record, and nothing else. Whatever he is writing at night, if he is writing, has not survived. The order of the two postings is not fixed by the record. In May 1917 the medical board strikes him off as unfit for further service after repeated relapses.
suggested_refs: Austro-Hungarian military medical service records, Vinkovci, Slavonia, 1915-1917

stops.name: Wolfratshausen, the death of the son called Peter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The reachable record gives only 'Peter (1907-ca. 1915)'. The place of death, the exact year and the age are not attested, and the Wolfratshausen setting is inference from the Jaffe family's country house
stops.campa: Somewhere in these war years the boy born to Else Jaffe at the end of 1907 dies, seven or eight years old, in the Bavarian countryside south of Munich where the affair that made him was conducted. He is buried under another man's surname. His father is in a Slavonian fever hospital or under guardianship or both, and cannot in any case attend the funeral of a child he was never permitted to claim. When he learned of it, and from whom, no document records.
suggested_refs: Bavarian civil registers for the Jaffe household, c. 1915; gap: no death record located
sources: gap noted: place, cause and exact date of Peter's death not attested

stops.name: Prague, at Max Brod's table
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1917; the German record dates his meeting with Kafka to a night train from Budapest to Prague in July. The coordinates are approximate: the gathering was at Max Brod's home, not at the Cafe Arco
stops.campa: In Prague he is a guest of Max Brod alongside Franz Kafka, Franz Werfel and Anton Kuh, and they plan a journal to be called Pages for the Struggle against the Will to Power. The title is aimed straight at Nietzsche: where Nietzsche read the will to power as the engine of life, Gross reads it as the wound the father inflicts and the son passes on. Kafka has met him days before, on a night train from Budapest, and is listening in his own way; readers of The Castle will find these corridors again. No issue of the journal has been located.
stops.quote: Er glaubte an die Herkunft alles Uebeln auf Erden von der Geschlechtsgewalt.
stops.quote_source: Anton Kuh, 'Die Lehre des Otto Gross', Neues Wiener Journal, 11 January 1921, p. 5
suggested_refs: The projected journal Blaetter zur Bekaempfung des Machtwillens, Prague, 1917; Franz Kafka, Das Schloss
sources: Anton Kuh, Neues Wiener Journal, 11 January 1921

stops.name: Graz, the guardianship lifted and reimposed
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1917 and for the restricted reimposition in December; the days are defaulted
stops.campa: In September the court lifts the guardianship. In December it puts it back, narrowed but real. Three months of legal adulthood at the age of forty, granted and withdrawn by an office in a city he stopped living in a decade ago. He has by now fathered five children by four women and published two psychiatric books, and the province of his birth holds that he cannot manage his own money. The December order is restricted; the file does not say restricted to what.
suggested_refs: Styrian court file on the lifting and partial reimposition of the Gross Kuratel, September and December 1917

stops.name: Friedenau, Berlin: the room at the Jungs'
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1919; the day is defaulted and the street address is not recorded
stops.campa: In October he comes back to Berlin for the last time and takes a room with Franz and Claere Jung in Friedenau, a novelist's household and not a physician's. Franz Jung had shared a Berlin room with him in 1913 and takes him in again. Since 1915 he has been writing for the anarchist paper Die freie Strasse, arguing that the war just ended was patriarchy's own logic carried to its conclusion. He has no practice, no income and no licence anyone would honour. He is forty-two, and has been taking cocaine for nineteen years.
suggested_refs: Die freie Strasse, Berlin, 1915-1919, Gross's contributions; the Franz and Claere Jung household in Friedenau

stops.name: Berlin, the passageway in February
stops.date_confidence: attested for 11 February 1920; the street and passageway are not named in the reachable sources
stops.campa: On the eleventh of February he is found in a Berlin passageway near a friends' warehouse, in withdrawal, starving, and frozen. Among those who reach him is the psychiatrist Hans Walter Gruhle, who knows exactly who is lying on the stones. It is a cold winter in a defeated city where a great many people are hungry, and nothing in the scene marks him out from any of them. The street and the passageway are not named in any source reached. They carry him across the city, north, to Pankow.
suggested_refs: Hans Walter Gruhle's account of finding Gross, Berlin, February 1920

stops.name: Pankow, Berlin: the clinic
stops.date_confidence: attested; the clinic's exact address in Pankow is not identified
stops.campa: He dies in a clinic at Pankow on the thirteenth of February, two days after they picked him up, of pneumonia on top of starvation and exposure. He is forty-two. He leaves five children by four women, and a body of writing scattered through anarchist papers that nobody will collect for sixty years. Freud will outlive him by nineteen years and Jung by forty-one. Where he is buried, no record reached says: no cemetery, no plot, no stone, only the death and the city.
stops.quote: So ist er auch dann schnell gestorben, nicht im Kompromiss, wie es fast zu erwarten war, nein, losgeloest von allen Menschen, die ihn bisher umgeben hatten, in einem riesenhaften Aufschwung von Schoepfer- und Denkkraft, die Leute begannen gerade zu ahnen, wer dieser Gross eigentlich war...
stops.quote_source: Franz Jung, in Brinkmann and Bose (eds.), Grosz/Jung/Grosz (Berlin, 1980), p. 105
suggested_refs: Berlin death register, 13 February 1920; gap: no cemetery or grave record located

stops.name: Vienna, Anton Kuh prints the doctrine
stops.date_confidence: attested; the essay appeared eleven months after Gross's death, not days after as is sometimes stated
stops.campa: Anton Kuh publishes an essay in the Neues Wiener Journal called The Teaching of Otto Gross, and prints the thing itself: that all evil on earth comes from sexual coercion, and that children raised without force between their parents would be brothers and sisters to one another. Kuh's sisters had nursed him at Bad Ischl, and Kuh himself had sat with him at Brod's table in Prague. He is the first to treat the dead man as a body of thought. The essay runs on page five, eleven months after the Pankow clinic.
stops.quote: Liebt euch ohne Gewalt, ihr Freien – und eure Kinder werden Geschwister sein!
stops.quote_source: Otto Gross, quoted by Anton Kuh, 'Die Lehre des Otto Gross', Neues Wiener Journal, 11 January 1921, p. 5
suggested_refs: Anton Kuh, 'Die Lehre des Otto Gross', Neues Wiener Journal, 11 January 1921, p. 5
sources: Anton Kuh, Neues Wiener Journal, 11 January 1921

stops.name: Kuesnacht, the credit in Psychological Types
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1921 publication; month and day unknown, defaulted. The Kuesnacht setting follows Jung's house and working address
stops.campa: A year after the death, in the house he built on the lake, Jung publishes Psychological Types and gives the world extraversion and introversion. Twice in the book he stops to say where the distinction came from: from the little Leipzig monograph of 1902, by the man he had diagnosed and been diagnosed by in the Burghoelzli thirteen years before, and who has been dead for a year. The two credits stand at paragraphs 466 and 879 of the Collected Works.
stops.quote: The relation he established between manic-depressive insanity and the type with a shallow consciousness shows that we are dealing with extraversion, while the relation between the psychology of the paranoiac and the type with a contracted consciousness indicates the identity with introversion.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung, Psychological Types (1921), Collected Works vol. 6, par. 879, on Otto Gross
suggested_refs: C. G. Jung, Psychological Types, CW 6, pars. 466 and 879
sources: C. G. Jung, Psychological Types, CW 6

stops.name: Berlin, the Bauhaus-Archiv: a society for the erased
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding congress of 28-30 May 1999; the society dissolved in 2017 and continues only as an informal working group
stops.campa: For six decades he is out of the record almost entirely. Then Martin Green's book on the Richthofen sisters appears in German in 1976, Emanuel Hurwitz publishes the first real biography in 1979, and in 1980 a publisher finally prints the selection of his writings that Franz Jung had assembled in 1923 and carried unpublished for fifty-seven years. In May 1999 a congress at the Bauhaus-Archiv in Berlin founds a society whose stated task is to find out why he was erased. It runs eighteen years and then dissolves.
suggested_refs: Internationale Otto Gross Gesellschaft e.V., founding congress, Bauhaus-Archiv Berlin, 28-30 May 1999; Emanuel Hurwitz, Otto Gross: Paradies-Sucher zwischen Freud und Jung (1979)

stops.name: Graz, the eighth congress comes home
stops.date_confidence: attested for 14-16 October 2011
stops.campa: The eighth international congress on his work convenes in Graz, the town of the gymnasium, the doctorate, the marriage, the habilitation and the court that took his legal personhood away, ninety-seven years after that court's ruling. The same year Vincent Cassel plays him in a Cronenberg film about the Freud and Jung rupture, and a wider audience meets him for ninety seconds as the patient who talks his doctor into taking his own desires seriously. Wilhelm Reich, who never met him, had taken the same thesis in the 1930s and built a sexual politics on it. The congress sits for three days and goes home.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the 8th International Otto Gross Congress, Graz, 14-16 October 2011; A Dangerous Method, dir. David Cronenberg, 2011
